description: Solo team: Nazifa Binte Hassan, Department of Urban and Regional Planning, BUET (Level-II Term-II), Dhaka. I work on spatial analysis and planning. For Space Apps 2026 I built FireBridge, which joins 25 years of NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspots into one record and a burning-activity calendar for Bangladesh. Skills: GIS, data analysis, Python, web mapping.
summary:
Bangladesh's satellite fire record appears to show burning jumping 186% after 2012. It didn't happen. Measured with Aqua MODIS alone — an instrument that did not change — burning actually fell about 30%. The 2012 jump is the day VIIRS replaced MODIS and began seeing smaller fires.

FireBridge removes that break. It converts every NASA FIRMS MODIS detection since 2000 into its VIIRS equivalent, weighted by season and 0.5° grid cell, and reproduces the unchanged-instrument trend to within 3.3 percentage points. Pick any area — the whole country, a drawn box, a point and radius — and any dates, and get a monthly burning-activity calendar, how that month compares with normal, the land cover and weather behind it, and a CSV.

It is built for forest officers, disaster managers and environment agencies. It updates itself every day from NASA GIBS with no API key, and it has already carried the record across the retirement of VIIRS S-NPP on 2 November 2026 by switching to NOAA-20. Run unchanged on Portugal, a Mediterranean wildfire regime it was never designed for, it reaches 19.7% monthly error against Bangladesh's 17.9%.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Bangladesh's satellite fire record says burning rose 186% after 2012. Aqua MODIS, an instrument that did not change, says it fell about 30%. Everything between those two numbers is the day NASA's VIIRS sensor replaced MODIS and began seeing smaller fires. For 14 years, anyone asking whether Bangladesh is burning more has been reading a sensor upgrade as an environmental trend.

That break sits on top of something real. Every spring thousands of fires burn here, 76% of them in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and 96% in March and April. Most are jhum: farmers clearing slopes before the monsoon. Some escape into forest, and the smoke reaches the cities. NASA has watched them since 2000 with MODIS (1 km pixels) and since 2012 with VIIRS (375 m). VIIRS finds about 3.6 times as many spring hotspots and up to 8 times as many in winter, so a trend that crosses 2012 is mostly a change of camera. On 2 November 2026 VIIRS S-NPP itself retired, opening a third break in the same record.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Filter: vegetation fires only (type 0; MODIS confidence 30 or more; VIIRS nominal and high). Brick kilns, gas flares and other static sources are set aside.

2. Convert: every MODIS detection is given a weight equal to the ratio of VIIRS S-NPP to MODIS counts for its season (Nov–Feb, Mar, Apr, May, Jun–Oct) and its 0.5° cell, learned on the 2012–2021 overlap with shrinkage toward the seasonal ratio. Terra-only years before July 2002 use a separate ratio and are marked low confidence. NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 are linked to S-NPP the same way.

3. Test: leave-one-year-out cross-validation. National monthly error falls from 44% with one fixed ratio to 18% with season × place weights; cell-level annual correlation is 0.93. On 2023–2025, years the model never saw, the converted count was within 3–7% of the real VIIRS count. Uncertainty bands are empirical 80% intervals (83% observed coverage).

CONTROL TEST: WAS THE 2012 JUMP REAL?

Aqua and Terra MODIS flew unchanged across the 2012 boundary, so a MODIS-only series is an instrument that did not change. Mean hotspots per year, 2003-2011 against 2013-2021 (the 2012 boundary year excluded): Aqua MODIS alone 2,922 to 2,041, a fall of 30.1%. Terra MODIS alone, a fall of 17.8%. The raw MODIS-then-VIIRS splice: 3,207 to 9,157, a rise of 185.5%. FireBridge harmonized: 12,514 to 9,157, a fall of 26.8%.

Burning in Bangladesh fell by about 30%. The raw splice reports a 186% rise, wrong by 216 percentage points and in the opposite direction. The harmonized series lands within 3.3 percentage points of the unchanged instrument, which is what the harmonization is supposed to reproduce. Aqua is the primary control: its 13:30 overpass is closest to S-NPP and its orbit was stable through 2021.

DOES THE METHOD TRAVEL? PORTUGAL

Bangladesh's five seasons are a Bangladesh decision, so for a fair cross-country test both countries are run through one identical, country-agnostic configuration: weight by calendar month and 0.5 degree cell, shrinkage, fitted on the 2012-2021 overlap, leave-one-year-out, nothing tuned per country.

Portugal is about as unlike Bangladesh as a fire regime gets: summer Mediterranean wildfire in forest and scrub against spring jhum burning on cultivated hillsides. National monthly error with a single ratio: Bangladesh 43.7%, Portugal 27.9%. Harmonized: Bangladesh 17.9%, Portugal 19.7%. The method travels, with nothing retuned.

The spatial refinement does not travel. Splitting the ratio by 0.5 degree cell improves cell-level error in Bangladesh (37.1% to 35.9%) and makes it clearly worse in Portugal (73.3% to 78.7%). The likely reason is that jhum fires return to the same fields year after year, so a cell's ratio is stable and worth learning, while Portugal's wildfires move, so last year's cell ratios are mostly noise. That is an interpretation, not a measurement. The rule it implies: add cells only where burning recurs in place, and use the month-only model where it moves.

Nepal was attempted as a third country and is not reported: NASA FIRMS timed out on six of its twenty files, leaving only three complete overlap years, too few for a cross-validated figure.

WHAT IS NEW HERE

Most harmonizations pick one conversion ratio and apply it everywhere. The ratio is not one number. In Bangladesh it is 3.5 in March and 8.2 in winter, and it differs between the hills and the delta, so FireBridge learns a separate weight for every season and every 0.5 degree cell and shrinks each one toward its season average where the data are thin.

Three further choices are unusual. The record is checked against an instrument that never changed, not only against itself, which is how we can say the 2012 rise was false rather than merely suspicious. The daily update reads NASA GIBS map tiles rather than a data feed, so it needs no API key, no quota and no account, and it kept running through the S-NPP shutdown. And the project publishes where it fails: the Sundarbans canopy, the Terra-only years, and the Portugal cell result above, which contradicts a design choice that works at home.

WHAT THE APP DOES

- One harmonized monthly record, Nov 2000 to today.

- Any area: whole country, preset areas, a drawn box or shape, or a point and radius; any date range.

- A burning-activity calendar (month × year), switchable between counts and difference from the median of reliable baseline years.

- A "how does this month compare" panel with rank, typical range and the weather of that month.

- Land cover of the burned pixels (MODIS MCD12Q1) and a weather test (NASA POWER rainfall, humidity, temperature, soil wetness, aerosol) with Spearman correlations and permutation p-values.

- CSV download of the selected record.

2026, LIVE AND KEYLESS

2026 data come from NASA GIBS VIIRS thermal anomaly vector tiles, sorted to Bangladesh by distance to past detections (99.2% recall, 98.5% precision on held-out days). A GitHub Action updates the site daily. When S-NPP stopped, NOAA-20 was converted and checked against ten months of 2026 overlap (94% of S-NPP).

WHAT WE FOUND

52% of hotspots fall on shrub, savanna and grass (mostly jhum fallow), 31% on forest, 15% on cropland. Humid Aprils have fewer April fires (ρ = −0.65, p < 0.001, 23 years). After a wet January–March, 67% of spring burning falls in April against 46% after a dry one: rain moves burning later rather than cancelling it, so FireBridge warns about timing, not totals.

WHO IT IS FOR

Forest Department: are the hill reserves burning early or heavily this year? Department of Environment: when will the smoke season peak? Disaster management: which weeks need crews ready? Agriculture extension and researchers: where is crop burning rising, and is it moving?

The useful output is timing. Bangladesh's critical weeks are March and April, and a month-by-month record that is finally comparable across 25 years lets an office say whether this April is early, heavy or normal while there are still weeks left to act. Asked before, the same question returned a number that mixed fire with sensor, which is why the honest answer used to be that nobody knew. The same two lines of code that made this work for Bangladesh work for Portugal, so any country with a FIRMS file can have the same answer.

LIMITS

Small fires under the Sundarbans canopy are mostly missed by both sensors. November 2000–June 2002 is low confidence. 2026 months are near-real-time and will be replaced by standard processing when FIRMS releases it.

NEXT

Portugal is validated above; the next step is to run more countries and publish a per-country report card, so a user can see the method's error for their own area before trusting it. Then: linking the season tracker to smoke and air quality, and field checks with forest offices.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy), HTML/JavaScript with Leaflet, GitHub Actions for the daily update, Vercel for hosting. Code: https://github.com/NBHassan09/firebridge

USE OF AI

Claude (Anthropic) was used as a coding, analysis and writing assistant under my direction: it wrote and ran the data pipeline and analysis, wrote the web app code, drafted text, and built the demo video animations and subtitles. The video voice-over is synthetic, generated with the open-source Kokoro text-to-speech model. All data are public NASA data.
